intro: This guide takes your group through The Pilgrim’s Progress (For Teens) in twelve weeks, one chapter a week. It retells John Bunyan’s great allegory for teenagers aged about 13 to 18, following Christian from the City of Destruction to the Celestial City and pausing to ask what each scene says about guilt, grace, peer pressure, doubt, drift and finishing well. It suits a youth group, a homeschool or a small group.

Each session takes about 30 to 40 minutes. Open by saying the memory verse together (3 minutes). Read the chapter, either aloud together or at home beforehand (5–10 minutes). Talk through the chapter’s three questions, which come with answers to help you (10 minutes). Do the activity (10 minutes). Then close by praying, in your own words or inviting a volunteer to pray, about what the chapter raised (2–3 minutes). Each chapter ends with a “One thing to do” challenge, which is worth reading out before people leave.

To prepare, read the chapter yourself and glance at the activity so you know what you need; most weeks need only paper and pens, or nothing at all. Bunyan does not soften the hard parts: Faithful is put to death at Vanity Fair, and in Doubting Castle Giant Despair urges the pilgrims to take their own lives. Read chapters 8 and 10 carefully beforehand, keep the talk calm and hopeful, and be ready to follow up privately with anyone who seems shaken. If a young person tells you they have had thoughts of harming themselves, take it seriously, stay with them and involve a trusted adult or professional. Throughout, let people keep personal reflection private and never press anyone to share more than they want to.

weeks.summary: A man in rags reads a book, feels the full weight of the burden on his back and cries, “What shall I do?” His family mock him and then ignore him, but Evangelist points him toward a shining light and a Wicket Gate, and he runs with his fingers in his ears, shouting, “Life! Life! Eternal life!” Obstinate refuses to think about it and goes home, while Pliable comes along on a wave of excitement. The big idea: the journey to God begins when we stop numbing the weight of our guilt and take it seriously.

memory_verse.text: For my iniquities have gone over my head; like a heavy burden, they are too heavy for me.

activity.title: Obstinate, Pliable or Christian?
steps: Read out the three responses from the chapter: Obstinate shuts the question down, Pliable says yes on a wave of feeling, Christian is serious and moves.
In small groups, think of everyday ways people today respond like Obstinate and like Pliable when faith comes up.
Share a few examples with the whole group, without naming real people.
Ask: what does the chapter suggest a serious response looks like?
Privately, write one sentence on which response is most like you at the moment, and keep it to yourself.

weeks.summary: Christian and Pliable fall into the Slough of Despond, the despair that floods in when a person first wakes up to what is wrong with them. Pliable claws his way out on the side nearest home and quits, while Christian keeps struggling toward the far side until Help pulls him out. Mr. Worldly Wiseman then persuades him to seek relief from Legality by simply being a respectable person, and Christian ends up under a fiery, overhanging hill until Evangelist sets him right. The big idea: early despair is not a reason to quit, and the easy, respectable shortcut cannot lift our guilt.

memory_verse.text: He drew me up from the pit of destruction, out of the miry bog, and set my feet upon a rock, making my steps secure.

activity.title: The Respectable Shortcut
activity.materials: A whiteboard or large sheet of paper
steps: Write two headings: “Worldly Wiseman’s offer” and “Why it fails.”
As a group, list ways people today try to get rid of guilt by just being a decent, respectable person.
Under the second heading, list what the chapter says goes wrong with that plan.
Discuss: why did the shortcut sound so mature and sensible to an exhausted Christian?
Ask everyone to name, silently to themselves, one person who points them toward God rather than the easy way.

weeks.summary: Christian knocks at the Wicket Gate, afraid he will be turned away, and Goodwill pulls him inside, saying they make no objections against anyone, no matter what they have done. His burden does not fall off yet; he must carry it to the place of deliverance. At the House of the Interpreter he sees a dusty room cleaned only by sprinkled water, the two boys Passion and Patience, and a man locked in an iron cage of despair who slowly hardened his own heart. The big idea: no one is too far gone to knock, and grace, not self-effort, makes a heart clean.

memory_verse.text: Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you.

activity.title: Which Room?
steps: Describe the three scenes briefly: the dusty room, Passion and Patience, and the man in the iron cage.
Split into three groups and give each group one scene.
Each group explains its scene in modern terms and gives an example of where teenagers meet that reality today.
Groups report back to everyone in a minute or two.
Ask each person to write down privately which scene unsettled them most and why.

weeks.summary: Christian climbs a path walled in by Salvation to a Cross with an open tomb below it, and as he comes up to the Cross his burden loosens, rolls down the hill and falls into the tomb. He weeps, leaps three times for joy, and three Shining Ones tell him his sins are forgiven, give him new clothes, and set a mark on his forehead with a sealed scroll to carry. Every earlier attempt to lose the burden failed; it falls only at the Cross, and before he has done anything good on the journey. The big idea: forgiveness is received by looking to what Jesus has done, not earned by trying harder.

memory_verse.text: He himself bore our sins in his body on the tree, that we might die to sin and live to righteousness. By his wounds you have been healed.

activity.title: Where the Burden Didn’t Fall
activity.materials: A whiteboard or large sheet of paper
steps: Draw a simple road with stations: the City, Evangelist’s advice, the Slough, Legality’s hill, the Gate, the Cross.
As a group, mark which station the burden fell off at and why it did not fall at the others.
Discuss the difference between “be good and God will accept you” and what happens to Christian here.
Read the memory verse slowly three times together.
Give a minute of silence for each person to thank God quietly in their own words.

weeks.summary: Christian climbs the Hill Difficulty while Formalist and Hypocrisy take the easy side paths and are never heard of again. He falls asleep at a rest-stop, loses his scroll and has to go back for it, then passes two chained lions that frightened Timorous and Mistrust into turning back. At the top, the House Beautiful welcomes him, gives him rest in a room called Peace and arms him from head to foot for the valley ahead. The big idea: the right road is often the hard one, carelessness costs us, and we need a community that knows and equips us.

memory_verse.text: Therefore, since we are surrounded by so great a cloud of witnesses, let us also lay aside every weight, and sin which clings so closely, and let us run with endurance the race that is set before us.

activity.title: Chained Lions
steps: Explain that the lions roared but were chained, and the men who turned back never got close enough to see.
Individually, list three things that often make young people give up on doing right or following God.
Pool the lists and sort them together into “real danger” and “chained lion”.
Discuss: what helps you get close enough to find out a lion is chained?
Ask everyone to think privately of one place where they can be truly known, their own House Beautiful.

weeks.summary: In the Valley of Humiliation Apollyon claims Christian, offers him a deal, then lists his real failures. Christian admits they are true but answers that the Prince he serves is merciful and ready to forgive, and after a long fight, knocked flat, he grabs his sword again and drives Apollyon away. In the Valley of the Shadow of Death he cannot use his sword, so he uses All-prayer, and is comforted by hearing another pilgrim ahead in the dark. The big idea: we answer accusation with Christ’s mercy, and in the dark we keep praying and remember we are not alone.

memory_verse.text: Even though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil, for you are with me; your rod and your staff, they comfort me.

activity.title: Answering the Accuser
steps: Read Christian’s reply to Apollyon aloud: “All this is true … but the Prince I serve is merciful and ready to forgive.”
In pairs, write three general accusations someone might hear in their head, such as “You always mess up,” without anything personal.
For each, write an answer in Christian’s pattern: admit what is true, then point to Christ’s forgiveness.
Share a few answers with the group.
Talk about the second valley: who is a “voice ahead in the dark” that has helped you, such as a book, a friend or an older Christian?

weeks.summary: Christian catches up with Faithful, and the road gets lighter now that they walk together. Faithful tells how Adam the First tempted him with his three daughters, the Lust of the Flesh, the Lust of the Eyes and the Pride of Life, and how Shame nearly beat him by making faith feel embarrassing, until he saw that Shame tells what people think, not what God thinks. Then Talkative, whose religion is all in his tongue, leaves offended when Faithful asks about his actual life. The big idea: do not let embarrassment rule you, and let your faith show in your life, not just your talk.

memory_verse.text: For whoever is ashamed of me and of my words in this adulterous and sinful generation, of him will the Son of Man also be ashamed when he comes in the glory of his Father with the holy angels.

activity.title: What Shame Says Now
steps: Read out Shame’s lines from the chapter: faith is a “low, sneaking business,” a tender conscience is “unmanly,” and so on.
In small groups, rewrite each line as it might sound today at school or online.
Next to each one, write the answer Faithful learned: what does God think?
Share the best rewrites and answers with the whole group.
Privately, write down one small way you will refuse to be ruled by embarrassment this week.

weeks.summary: Evangelist warns the two pilgrims that a hard town is coming and one of them will die there. Vanity Fair sells everything, sits right across the road to the City, and is thrown into uproar by two men who dress and speak differently and answer every seller, “We buy the truth.” They are beaten and caged, and after a rigged trial Faithful is put to death, but a chariot carries him the nearest way to the celestial gate while Christian survives and walks on. The big idea: following Jesus may cost us, but what the world calls losing is winning in God’s eyes.

memory_verse.text: Do not fear what you are about to suffer… Be faithful unto death, and I will give you the crown of life.

activity.title: What’s for Sale?
steps: Ask everyone to write on sticky notes things today’s world sells as a way to “be someone”, one per note: a look, a status, a number of followers and so on.
Stick them on a wall to make a market stall.
As a group, discuss which ones are hardest to walk past without buying, and why.
Talk about why the fair was so angry at two people who simply weren’t interested.
Invite each person to choose privately one thing they will refuse to “buy” for a set time this week.

weeks.summary: Hopeful joins Christian after watching how he and Faithful suffered. They meet By-ends, who follows religion only when it walks “in his silver slippers” and never against wind and tide, and his friends from Love-gain, who use faith to get rich; Christian answers that this is the religion of Judas. At the Hill Lucre, Demas calls them to a silver mine; Christian refuses, but By-ends and his friends turn aside and are never seen again, and the pilgrims pass Lot’s wife, turned to a pillar of salt for looking back. The big idea: we cannot serve God and money, and true faith follows Christ when it costs as well as when it pays.

memory_verse.text: No one can serve two masters, for either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will be devoted to the one and despise the other. You cannot serve God and money.

activity.title: Silver Slippers or Rags?
steps: Mark one side of the room “Silver slippers” (faith that pays off) and the other “Rags” (faith that costs).
Read out situations, such as praying before lunch in front of friends, or standing up for someone unpopular, and ask people to stand where each would fall.
After each one, ask: would By-ends turn up for this?
Discuss why Christian insisted on owning religion in its rags.
Challenge everyone to do one thing for God this week that brings no audience or advantage.

weeks.summary: Tired of stony ground, Christian leads Hopeful over a fence into By-path Meadow, and they end up lost in a storm and asleep in the grounds of Doubting Castle. Giant Despair throws them into a dungeon, beats them and, on his wife’s advice, urges them to end their own lives; Hopeful keeps Christian going by reminding him of all he has survived. After a night of prayer Christian remembers the key called Promise in his chest, which opens every lock, and they walk free. The big idea: despair lies, God’s promises are the key out, and no one should face the dark alone.

memory_verse.text: Let us hold fast the confession of our hope without wavering, for he who promised is faithful.

activity.title: Keys Called Promise
steps: Remind the group that Christian had the key the whole time but had forgotten it.
Together, list some of God’s promises you know from the Bible, and look up any you are unsure of.
Each person writes one promise on a card to keep in a pocket, phone case or wallet.
Discuss: who are the “Hopefuls” in our lives, and how can we be one for a friend?
Make sure everyone knows who they can talk to if they ever feel in the dungeon, and mention that you are available.

weeks.summary: On the Delectable Mountains the shepherds show the pilgrims hard sights: the cliff of Error, the blind men of Caution caught by Giant Despair, and a by-way to hell for hypocrites who kept up a show of pilgrimage for a long time. The pilgrims meet Ignorance, who trusts his decent life rather than the gate, and recall Little-Faith, who was robbed but kept his jewels and arrived. On the Enchanted Ground, Hopeful wants to nap, but Christian refuses and they stay awake by talking about how Hopeful came to God. The big idea: the quiet danger is drift, and we stay awake by staying engaged with others on the road.

memory_verse.text: So then let us not sleep, as others do, but let us keep awake and be sober.

activity.title: Signs of Drift
steps: Explain that the Enchanted Ground does not feel dangerous; it just makes you sleepy.
In small groups, list early warning signs that someone is drifting from God rather than rebelling.
Then list practical things that keep a person awake, drawing on how Christian and Hopeful kept talking.
Share the lists and agree on the three best ideas.
Challenge each person to have one real conversation about faith with someone this week.

weeks.summary: In the land of Beulah the pilgrims see the Celestial City, but must cross a deep river with no bridge, which is death. Christian nearly drowns, overwhelmed by darkness and old sins, until Hopeful holds him up, saying he feels the bottom and it is good, and Christian grasps the promise that God will be with him through the waters. They are welcomed into the City with trumpets and bells, but Ignorance, ferried across by Vain-Hope, reaches the gate with no certificate, showing there is a way to hell even from the gate of heaven. The big idea: our hope must rest on what Christ did at the Cross, not on our own decent life.

memory_verse.text: When you pass through the waters, I will be with you; and through the rivers, they shall not overwhelm you; when you walk through fire you shall not be burned, and the flame shall not consume you.

activity.title: Looking Back on the Road
steps: As a group, list the main places of the journey from the City of Destruction to the Celestial City.
Ask each person to choose the scene that has stayed with them most and say why, if they are happy to.
Discuss the difference between Christian, who struggled in the river, and Ignorance, who crossed easily but had no certificate.
Ask: what is the “certificate” the book is talking about?
Give everyone a few minutes to write privately what they want to remember from the whole book.
